questions.title: Why can't an employee sue for 'average daily wage penalties' under Minn. Stat. § 181.101 if the statute says money collected goes to the employee?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the court's interpretation of the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act (MPWA). The statute says that if the Commissioner collects a penalty, the money must be paid to the employee. It seems logical that this implies the employee has a right to seek those penalties directly if the Commissioner doesn't act. However, the court ruled that only the Commissioner can seek these penalties because the text explicitly grants that power to the Commissioner. How does the court distinguish between who *collects* the money versus who has the *cause of action* to initiate the penalty? Is this a strict textualist reading where 'expressio unius est exclusio alterius' applies?

questions.title: How does voluntary cessation of an illegal policy affect Article III standing when seeking civil penalties payable to the state?
questions.question_body: In the MFLSA portion of the opinion, the court vacates summary judgment to check for mootness regarding statutory penalties. I understand that voluntary cessation usually doesn't moot a case seeking injunctive relief, but here Cohen is seeking civil penalties that would be paid to the Commissioner, not him. Since he already got his back wages and liquidated damages, does he still have a 'personal stake' in the outcome sufficient for standing under *Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw*? If the penalty doesn't compensate him personally, how does stopping the violation make his claim for those specific penalties moot?

questions.title: What is the procedural difference between raising a new claim for injunctive relief in a summary judgment brief versus amending the complaint?
questions.question_body: The court dismissed Cohen's request for an injunction ordering Consilio to rescind its 2019 policy because he didn't raise it until his summary judgment briefing, having withdrawn earlier requests in his complaint. I know Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15 governs amendments, but why couldn't the court just treat his briefing as a motion to amend or consider it liberally since it's related to the original wage theft allegations? At what point in litigation is it too late to pivot from seeking monetary damages to seeking specific equitable relief without formally amending pleadings?

questions.title: Did Cohen waive his MWTA notice claim by failing to cite specific statutory authority for penalties in his appeal?
questions.question_body: Regarding the Minnesota Wage Theft Act (MWTA) claim, the court affirmed dismissal partly because Cohen pointed to 'no statutory authority allowing for civil penalties' and offered 'no meaningful argument.' The court cites *Milligan* regarding waiver. My confusion is: Was this a failure of pleading (not stating a valid cause of action initially) or a failure of appellate advocacy (waiver by not briefing it properly)? If a statute allows penalties generally but not specifically for notice violations, is that a jurisdictional bar or just a merits defeat that shouldn't be waived so easily?

questions.title: Why did Judge Kobes concur specially regarding attorney's fees and costs if they weren't explicitly discussed in the majority opinion?
questions.question_body: Judge Kobes mentions in his special concurrence that he also vacates the ruling on attorney's fees, costs, and prejudgment interest, yet these issues don't seem to appear in Part II of Judge Kelly's majority opinion. Are these items automatically tied to the underlying MFLSA claim such that vacating the main claim necessitates vacating fee awards? Or did Kobes identify an error that the majority overlooked, and if so, why didn't the majority address it directly?

questions.title: How does Minnesota's legislative history regarding discharged vs. resigned employees influence statutory interpretation of penalty rights?
questions.question_body: The court relies heavily on comparing § 181.101 with §§ 181.13 and 181.14. The latter two sections explicitly allow employees who are discharged or quit to charge and collect penalties themselves. The court uses this contrast ('knows how') to argue that because § 181.101 lacks similar language for general wage non-payment, employees cannot seek penalties there. Is this canon of construction (*nosci tur a sociis* or similar) strong enough to override potential equitable arguments that employees should always have direct access to penalties when commissioners are overloaded?
